fixes.explanation: That's exactly it, baker. The rich man says, "What is this I hear about you? Turn in an account of your management, for you cannot be manager any longer." (Luke 16:2) He asks for the books and tells the manager the job is ending. Basically, "hand me the paperwork."

Right, baker. The manager says, "I am too weak to dig and too ashamed to beg." (Luke 16:3) He names both options and crosses them off in one sentence. That's a man with a lot of thinking to do, and he's about to do it.

You got it, baker. The manager says, "I know what I will do so that after my removal from management, people will welcome me into their homes." (Luke 16:4) He's already planning for after his removal. Say what you want about him, the man does not sit around waiting.
Nope, the manager goes the other direction. He says, "Take your bill, sit down quickly, and write fifty." (Luke 16:6) Nobody is told to pay the full hundred. The manager tells him to write fifty.

Whoa, friend, that would make for a very short list of new friends. The manager tells the debtor to "write fifty," not two hundred. (Luke 16:6) The bill he has him write goes from a hundred measures down to fifty.

Plot twist, baker. "The master commended the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly." (Luke 16:8) A commendation is not what I'd have expected from that master. The text still calls him the dishonest manager, so the shrewdness is what gets commended.

Honestly, I'd have bet on this one too. But the text says, "The master commended the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly." (Luke 16:8) Prison isn't mentioned anywhere, only a commendation. That's what makes this story so surprising.

That's a sensible guess, friend, since the manager changed those bills. But the text never mentions repayment. It says, "The master commended the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly." (Luke 16:8) The master's response is a commendation.

Bigger barns are the plan of a rich man in another story, friend (Luke 12:18). In Jesus' words here, it's, "…use worldly wealth to make friends for yourselves…" (Luke 16:9) Bigger barns aren't in this passage at all. Friends are.

That's right, baker. Jesus says to use worldly wealth to make friends "…so that when it is gone, they will welcome you into eternal dwellings." (Luke 16:9) Notice the "…when it is gone…" The wealth is gone, and the dwellings Jesus names are eternal.

I see why you picked it, but it's the opposite of what Jesus says. He says, "…whoever is dishonest with very little will also be dishonest with much." (Luke 16:10) Jesus pairs it with the other half of the line: "Whoever is faithful with very little will also be faithful with much…" The little and the much go together.

That's it, baker. Jesus asks, "So if you have not been faithful with worldly wealth, who will entrust you with true riches?" (Luke 16:11) He puts worldly wealth and true riches in the same question. The thing to fill in is "true riches."

That phrase belongs to another moment, friend. Jesus says to Peter, one of His disciples, "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven…" (Matthew 16:19) Here the question is about who will entrust you with "true riches." (Luke 16:11)

Yes, baker. Jesus asks, "And if you have not been faithful with the belongings of another, who will give you belongings of your own?" (Luke 16:12) He sets belongings of another next to belongings of your own. The word that fills the blank is "own."
